resources.title: What is Gluten Anyway? (America's Test Kitchen Kids)
resources.why: A recipe tester makes 'webbed proteins' easy to picture, so you can see why only wheat dough can trap gas like a balloon.

resources.title: Science of Bread: Bread Science 101 (Exploratorium)
resources.why: It compares gluten to the rubber of a balloon and shows how starch reinforces it, which explains in a few minutes why rice flour falls flat.

resources.title: Gluten free rice-flour bread could revolutionize global bread production (ScienceDaily)
resources.why: Researchers got rice-flour bread to rise with no gluten at all, and how they did it shows exactly what gluten normally does.

resources.title: Baking Bread: The Chemistry of Bread-Making (Compound Interest)
resources.why: A one-page infographic that shows flour proteins, water, enzymes and yeast all working toward a risen loaf.

resources.title: The Only Video You'll Ever Need to Watch About Gluten (Reactions)
resources.why: The American Chemical Society's channel breaks gluten into its two proteins and explains, molecule by molecule, why dough both stretches and snaps back.

resources.title: Gluten: How Does It Work? (Modernist Cuisine)
resources.why: The rubber-band image (gliadin lets dough stretch, glutenin makes it snap back) will change how you think about every dough you knead.

resources.title: The structure and properties of gluten: an elastic protein from wheat grain (Shewry et al., Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B)
resources.why: This is the classic primary source for the 'elastic backbone' idea, and its 'loop and train' model of how glutenin stores springiness is easy to picture.

resources.title: How a Chemist Makes the Softest Bread You'll Ever Eat
resources.why: The tangzhong trick (pre-cooking some flour with water) shows starch grabbing water and turning it into a softer loaf.

resources.title: What is Starch Gelatinization?
resources.why: A short look at what happens inside starch granules when dough turns into crumb in the oven.

resources.title: Damaged Starch (BAKERpedia)
resources.why: Granules broken in the mill soak up 2–3 times more water and feed the yeast, so the way flour is milled quietly changes your dough.

resources.title: The Chemistry of Breadmaking (open-access review)
resources.why: A free review that follows amylose and amylopectin from dough through baking to staling, for when you want the full story.

resources.title: Thursday Thoughts: Baking With Enzymes
resources.why: A baker explains how the enzymes already in flour (and the ones mills add) change dough before the yeast even gets going.

resources.title: Enzymatic Activity (Alpha-Amylase) in Flour & Its Impact on Dough (Pizza Blab)
resources.why: Too much native amylase, from wheat that sprouted in the field, gives a gummy crumb that seems underbaked, and the 'falling number' test catches it.

resources.title: Enzymes in Bread Baking: What They Are, How They Work (BAKERpedia e-book)
resources.why: A free, plain-language guide to amylases and the xylanases that break down arabinoxylans, the 'minor' fibre that holds up to a quarter of the water in dough.

resources.title: Bread chemistry on the rise (Chemistry World)
resources.why: A chemist's tour of the less-famous parts of flour, such as the lipids that sit at bubble surfaces and keep gas cells from merging.

resources.title: Expert's Guide to Flour Types (America's Test Kitchen)
resources.why: Jack Bishop shows side by side how a few points of protein take you from tender cake to chewy loaf.

resources.title: What is baker's math, and how can I use it in my everyday bread baking? (King Arthur)
resources.why: Once flour is always 100%, you can compare any two recipes at a glance and see why each flour needs a different amount of water.

resources.title: Science of Cooking: Ask the Inquisitive Cooks! (Exploratorium)
resources.why: Whole wheat flour has more protein yet makes denser bread, because sharp flakes of bran cut the gluten strands as they form.

resources.title: Wheat flour (Wikipedia)
resources.why: A handy reference for how hard and soft wheats are graded into flour types and protein ranges in different countries.

resources.title: Science: What happens when you wash a Dough? Here's how to see and feel gluten
resources.why: Watch a ball of dough rinsed under water until the starch runs off and only a stretchy, gummy lump of gluten is left.

resources.title: Science of Bread: Great Balls of Gluten Activity (Exploratorium)
resources.why: A kitchen experiment you can do in 20 minutes that proves gluten only exists once water and kneading build it.

resources.title: Which Wheat Flour Has the Most Gluten? (Science Buddies)
resources.why: Turns the dough-washing test into a real experiment: weigh the gluten balls from different flours and check them against the labels.

resources.title: A beginner's guide to gluten (King Arthur)
resources.why: It explains why dry flour holds only the two proteins and water is what turns them into gluten.
